title: The Sage's Secret to Boundless Health (HI)
summary: Akbar asks an ancient centenarian for the secret to a century of vibrant health. Birbal summarizes the rules of living well.
full_text:
Emperor Akbar was visited by a venerable sage from the foothills of the Himalayas who had reached the age of one hundred and ten years, yet walked upright with firm steps, had sharp eyesight, all his natural teeth, and a clear, resonant voice.

Akbar, who often suffered from gout, indigestion, and fatigue, asked in awe: 'Revered elder! What rare herbal elixir, pearl tonic, or secret gold potion have you taken to preserve your youth for over a century?'

The old sage smiled and replied: 'Your Majesty, I have never swallowed a single grain of gold powder or tasted an imperial tonic. My medicine is written in the simple laws of daily life:

'First, eat only when genuinely hungry, and always stop while one-fourth of your stomach is still empty.

'Second, walk two leagues every day beneath the open sky, letting sweat carry away the impurities of the flesh.

'Third, sleep with the birds at sunset, and wake with the sun at dawn.

'Fourth, harbor no hatred, jealousy, or revenge in your breast, for bitterness poisons the blood more than venom.

'And fifth, laugh heartily every day with children and friends, for joy is the true fountain of youth.'

Akbar turned to Birbal: 'Is it truly so simple, Birbal? Can health be maintained without the court physicians' expensive syrups?'

Birbal said with a gentle bow:

'Sire, human beings love complexity because it allows them to purchase health with money rather than discipline!

'A wealthy emperor prefers to swallow expensive gold pills rather than stop overeating rich saffron meats!

'He prefers to ride in velvet carriages rather than walk on his own feet, and he allows anger and ambition to boil his blood, expecting medicine to cool the fever!

'Nature demands no gold for health; she demands only moderation, clean water, physical movement, and a peaceful, cheerful heart. He who obeys nature lives long and dies in peace.'

Akbar took the sage's rules to heart, reduced the rich dishes at court banquets, walked daily in his gardens, and experienced vibrant renewed health.
